title: Global Health Equity Considerations of Political Decisions: Trump, The US, and Immunization
authors: Juan Pablo Gutiérrez, Brian Wahl, Susanna Lehtimaki, Nina Schwalbe
summary: The paper examines how political choices on global health funding affect the four key dimensions of vaccination and immunization in LMICs: access, affordability, availability, and acceptability. It shows how reductions in investment and shifting priorities risk undermining vaccination programs and essential health services. By analyzing these dynamics, the paper highlights the growing threats to health equity and underscores the need for stronger international cooperation, sustained financing, and policy measures that can protect and expand equitable access to care in the face of political change.

title: Adoption of pandemic treaty is historic: Compliance and accountability must now follow
authors: Taran K Deol, Elliot Hannon, Susanna Lehtimaki, Matthew M Kavanagh, Nina Schwalbe
summary: The Pandemic Treaty adopted at the 78th World Health Assembly (WHA78) is a landmark achievement in global health. Adoption is just a first step. As negotiators continue to work on Pathogen Access and Benefits Sharing, preparing, preventing, and responding to the next pandemic will require accountability by Member States towards their commitments. Experience shows voluntary reporting often fails; monitoring implementation will enable progress and accountability to be tracked transparently.

title: The pandemic treaty: A forensic review of process and pitfalls
authors: Nina Schwalbe, Susanna Lehtimaki, Elliot Hannon
summary: This article examines efforts to develop a pandemic treaty through World Health Organization member state agreement from 2021 to 2025, focusing on challenges during the process. The COVID-19 pandemic showed the critical need for strong global agreements to prepare for and respond to health crises, with relevance for policymakers and researchers. The analysis highlights practical steps for future negotiations, including stronger political engagement, better coordination, greater transparency, and ensuring a broader range of voices and stakeholders are included.

title: Pandemic treaty is a win for multilateralism and global health
authors: Nina Schwalbe
summary: The World Health Organization's new Pandemic Agreement marks a historic step toward global health security and equity. Reached after three years of negotiations, the Treaty outlines commitments to strengthen health systems, improve access to pandemic tools, and tackle disease outbreaks at their source. While key issues like pathogen access and benefit sharing remain unresolved and financing mechanisms are weak, the Agreement lays a foundation for stronger multilateral action, despite waning support from major donors. As countries prepare to ratify and implement the treaty, the challenge will be turning this political consensus into real-world readiness.

title: The lessons New York still has not learned from the Covid vaccine rollout
authors: Nina Schwalbe
summary: New York's early COVID-19 vaccine rollout failed its most vulnerable residents. Drawing on firsthand experience and data, this article reports how older adults in low-income neighborhoods were left behind. New York's speed-first strategy came at a cost: no transportation, no home visits, and no real outreach for those at highest risk. On paper, coverage rates looked good, but the reality told a different story. A full public review of the city's pandemic response is long overdue.

title: Why we need a pandemic treaty now
authors: Nina Schwalbe
summary: With just one week of formal negotiations left, the world may be nearing its last chance to secure a global pandemic treaty that strengthens preparedness and response. Despite legal assurances that national sovereignty will be respected, negotiations remain stalled over key issues like equitable access to vaccines, data sharing, and commitments to One Health. Finalizing the treaty now would be a powerful affirmation of global solidarity and multilateralism.

title: Achieving gender justice for global health equity: the Lancet Commission on gender and global health
authors: Sarah Hawkes, Elhadj As Sy, Gary Barker, Frances Elaine Baum, Kent Buse, and Nina Schwalbe, among others
summary: Achieving gender justice in global health has the potential to improve health outcomes, reduce inequities, and transform workplaces and governance. Yet gender has become a polarizing concept, and efforts to advance gender justice face active opposition. This multidisciplinary Commission analyzes the historical, political, legal, and economic forces shaping gender and health, identifies how power imbalances and interest groups obstruct progress, and offers evidence-informed recommendations to incorporate gender justice into policy and practice.

title: An 'impact hub' approach to transforming global maternal health outcomes by 2030
authors: Mary-Ann Etiebet, Anne-Marie Slaughter, Lia Tadesse Gebredhin, Gordan LaForge, Alaa Murabit, Nina Schwalbe
summary: Preventing maternal mortality remains a persistent global challenge. Eliminating preventable deaths requires more than isolated success stories, it demands a coordinated, systemic approach rooted in equity, local solutions, and sustainable partnerships. As part of Brookings Institution's annual 17 Rooms flagship initiative, this piece explores how 'impact hubs' could serve as a bold new model to bring funders, governments, and local partners together to accelerate progress on maternal health.

title: Mpox: Neglect has led to a more dangerous virus now spreading across borders
authors: Christine McNab, Els Torreele, Ayoade Alakija, and Nina Schwalbe, among others
summary: The ongoing mpox outbreaks in Africa, driven by various clades including a newly identified Ib variant, are a severe concern. Despite mpox being endemic in several African countries for years, international attention surged only when clade IIb spread to wealthy nations in 2022. African outbreaks, where cases have surpassed 17,000 and led to 517 deaths in 2024 alone, have been largely neglected. Urgent action, political leadership, and significant financial support are needed to contain the spread and prevent future pandemics.

title: The pandemic agreement: Achieving an African win for health security inequity
authors: Nicaise Ndembi, Nebiyu Dereje, Fifa A. Rahman, and Nina Schwalbe, among others
summary: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the frailty and disparities of global health systems, especially in Africa. Vaccine nationalism and lack of inclusivity characterized early responses, raising concerns about global health security frameworks like the International Health Regulations. In response, the WHO formed an Intergovernmental Negotiating Body to draft a new Pandemic Agreement aimed at ensuring equity and addressing policy gaps. While progress has been made on governance, compliance, and R&D, consensus on pathogen access, benefit sharing, and financing remains elusive.
source: Journal of Public Health in Africa 2024

title: Beyond "business as usual": Lessons from FIFA for fair benefit-sharing in global health
authors: Brian Wahl, Gabriel Butin, Spring Gombe, Nina Schwalbe
summary: Researchers and agencies from low- and middle-income countries often contribute significantly to public health data but lack adequate compensation. Incentivizing data sharing is crucial for effective pandemic response, yet current legal frameworks have limitations. This piece explores adapting FIFA's benefit-sharing model, which rewards grassroots contributions and redistributes benefits, to global health.

title: From lemming to leader: Moving beyond Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to bring health financing assistance into the 21st century
authors: Tiffany Nassiri-Ansari, Nina Schwalbe, Susanna Lehtimaki
summary: Nearly 90 years after GDP was introduced to measure economic growth, there are increasing calls to stop using it and GNI for broader purposes, such as determining eligibility for development assistance. These measures prioritize economic growth over population health, masking inequalities. Alternatives like New Zealand's Living Standards Framework and the Multidimensional Poverty Index offer more nuanced assessments of well-being and poverty.

title: Assessing New York City's COVID-19 Vaccine Rollout Strategy: A Case for Risk-Informed Distribution
authors: Nina Schwalbe, Marta C. Nunes, Clare Cutland, Brian Wahl, Daniel Reidpath
summary: This study reviews the impact of early COVID-19 vaccine eligibility policies on coverage and outcomes in New York City. Using data from the Census Bureau and New York City Health, the authors assessed vaccination coverage and COVID-19 mortality rates among those aged 65+ across 177 zip code tabulation areas. Low-income areas with high proportions of older people had lower vaccination rates and higher mortality compared to wealthier areas.

title: Governance provisions in the WHO Pandemic Agreement draft
authors: Nina Schwalbe, Elliot Hannon, Lynda Gilby, Susanna Lehtimaki
summary: The WHO Pandemic Agreement draft lacks sufficient accountability measures. While it introduces a Conference of the Parties (COP) for governance, crucial details such as review scope and consequences for non-compliance remain unclear. Without a clear accountability mechanism, relying solely on good faith may not ensure effective implementation, as seen in the COVID-19 response.

title: Shaping Global Health Law through United Nations Governance: The UN High-Level Meeting on Pandemic PPR
authors: Benjamin Mason Meier, Alexandra Finch, Nina Schwalbe
summary: The UN General Assembly High-Level Meeting on pandemic prevention, preparedness, and response failed to garner significant high-level commitment and momentum for global health emergency governance. This article explores the UN's evolving role in global health governance and evaluates the contributions and shortcomings of the resulting Political Declaration.

title: Getting in Formation: WHO Constitutional Heads of Power and the Pandemic Agreement
authors: Alexandra L Phelan, Nina Schwalbe
summary: WHO Member States are nearing the end of negotiations for a proposed Pandemic Agreement, considering whether to adopt it under Article 19 or Article 21 of the WHO Constitution. While this may seem a simple 'opt in' or 'opt out' question, the legal and normative realities are more nuanced and require careful consideration by negotiators.

title: The new pandemic treaty: Are we in safer hands? Probably not
authors: Nina Schwalbe, Elliot Hannon, Susanna Lehtimaki
summary: The latest draft of the pandemic treaty falls short of expectations with governance revisions that lack accountability measures, leaving oversight to Member States through a World Health Assembly committee. Without robust compliance mechanisms and independent oversight, the treaty risks being ineffective in addressing the multisectoral challenges of pandemic preparedness and response.

title: WHO Member States are negotiating a Pandemic Treaty. But will countries follow the new rules?
authors: Elliot Hannon, Nina Schwalbe, Susanna Lehtimaki
summary: An independent monitoring mechanism is essential for the Pandemic Accord. Negotiators must remember to keep Member States accountable. It's feasible, viable, achievable and vital for preparing for the inevitable next pandemic.

title: Where there is a will, there is a way: independent assessment of member state compliance with the pandemic agreement
authors: Susanna Lehtimaki, Elliot Hannon, Layth Hanbali, Daniela-Filipa Soltan, Kimberley Peek, Tiffany Nassiri-Ansari, Nina Schwalbe
summary: On Oct 16, the world got its first glimpse of the complete draft negotiating text of the proposed pandemic agreement. In analysis of the preliminary draft, the authors found gaps in crucial areas such as health system resilience and equal access, and note the lack of an independent accountability mechanism. They assert the necessity of establishing a dedicated, independently mandated monitoring committee to ensure compliance.

title: Independent monitoring and the new pandemic agreement
authors: Layth Hanbali, Elliot Hannon, Susanna Lehtimaki, Christine McNab, Nina Schwalbe
summary: Negotiations are ongoing at the WHO for a binding pandemic prevention agreement, but past agreements haven't guaranteed effective implementation. While enforcement mechanisms are crucial, they're inconsistently applied and often rely on softer political approaches rather than strict legal measures. The authors propose an independent monitoring mechanism to assess and report on countries' adherence to the pandemic agreement.

title: Primary health care: a cornerstone of pandemic prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery
authors: Arush Lal, Nina Schwalbe
summary: The COVID-19 crisis highlighted the devastating consequences of neglecting primary health care before, during, and after a pandemic. This regression created a vicious cycle of vulnerability, especially for groups at high risk of disease. Primary health care should not be an afterthought, it must be core to pandemic prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery.

title: We cannot give up on the global pandemic treaty
authors: Nina Schwalbe
summary: Nearly two years after countries agreed to develop a new pandemic treaty, the prospect of achieving a bold new global agreement to prepare and respond to future disease threats is slipping away. The UN General Assembly's High-Level Meeting on Pandemics in September may be the last chance for political leaders to show the sustained commitment necessary to prevent and respond to future pandemics.

title: Bold moves for vaccine manufacturing equity
authors: Nina Schwalbe, Ole Kristian Aars
summary: The COVID-19 pandemic resulted in an unprecedented global crisis, and although there was unprecedented speed in developing new vaccines, the benefits from licensing effective vaccines in record time were not felt by all. More equitable distribution of vaccines requires an ecosystem that supports sustainable manufacturing capabilities to produce them locally.

title: Independent monitoring for the pandemic accord: a non-negotiable provision
authors: Layth Hanbali, Susanna Lehtimaki, Elliot Hannon, Christine McNab, Nina Schwalbe
summary: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the need for a coordinated global response to pandemics. In response, the Intergovernmental Negotiating Body for a pandemic accord discussed a zero draft in February 2023. Based on a comprehensive literature review of 11 monitoring mechanisms and expert consultation, the authors propose the establishment of an independent monitoring committee to assess state parties' compliance.

title: We need a pandemic treaty — but it must hold nations accountable
authors: Nina Schwalbe, Elliot Hannon
summary: The cycle of state denial and downplaying followed by disastrous consequences is a familiar pattern in public health crises, as demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic. To prevent similar outcomes in the future, it is crucial to establish a robust global pandemic treaty that emphasizes accountability and compliance to enhance preparedness and response efforts worldwide.

title: We need a new global compact on vaccines
authors: Nina Schwalbe
summary: Amid the emergence of monkeypox cases in the US and Europe, efforts are underway to vaccinate populations using the smallpox vaccine, which offers some cross-protection but is in limited supply. The global vaccine production model favors affluent Western nations over Africa, where monkeypox has circulated for decades without adequate vaccine deployment, highlighting the need for significant changes in vaccine manufacturing and distribution.

title: Strengthening Gavi is a way forward for global vaccine equity
authors: Nina Schwalbe
summary: The upcoming Biden administration COVID-19 summit shone a spotlight on global vaccine equity failure, where only 16% of people in low-income countries were vaccinated, compared to 80% in high-income nations. Lessons from Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, suggest strengthening its role by negotiating equity provisions in vaccine procurement contracts and investing in local vaccine manufacturing training.

title: Why we still need a pandemic treaty
authors: Elliot Hannon, Layth Hanbali, Susanna Lehtimaki, Nina Schwalbe
summary: The 2022 World Health Assembly saw Member States discussing amendments to the International Health Regulations. Despite meeting in person for the first time since COVID-19, little progress was made on solutions for future pandemics due to procedural focus. This article highlights the historical background and limitations of the IHR and proposes committing to a pandemic treaty to be prepared for the next pandemic.

title: Use of financial incentives to increase adult vaccination coverage: A narrative review of lessons learned from COVID-19
authors: Nina Schwalbe, Layth Hanbali, Marta C Nunes, Susanna Lehtimaki
summary: To encourage COVID-19 vaccination, governments have offered a wide range of incentives ranging from cash to cows. This narrative review sought to understand the evidence base informing these programs and the extent to which they are effective. Evidence showed cash transfers increased coverage and intention to be vaccinated, though improvements were limited; non-cash incentives such as lotteries did not appear to have an impact.

title: Increasing efficiency in vaccine production: A primer for change
authors: Ole Kristian Aars, Michael Clark, Nina Schwalbe
summary: The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the importance of vaccines as public health and pandemic preparedness tools and amplified issues ranging from equitable distribution to reliable supply. Delays in time from the first dose in a high-income country to introduction at scale in a low-income country can take years. This paper provides an overview of the vaccine research and development process and where reform of the current system could increase access.

title: Evidence on Digital Mental Health Interventions for Adolescents and Young People: Systematic Overview
authors: Susanna Lehtimaki, Jana Martic, Brian Wahl, Katherine Foster, Nina Schwalbe
summary: Although digital interventions for mental health can be effective for both supplementing and supplanting traditional treatment, only a small proportion of existing digital platforms are evidence based. Their cost-effectiveness, including in low- and middle-income countries, has been understudied. Widespread adoption will require more rigorous and consistent demonstrations of effectiveness relative to the type of service and population.

title: The World Should Treat Pandemics Like It Treats Chemical Weapons
authors: Nina Schwalbe, Susanna Lehtimaki
summary: While the world was still battling COVID-19, it was time to start preparing for the next pandemic, above all, how to prevent it. This piece argues for taking pandemic containment as seriously as other dangers of mass destruction, such as nuclear proliferation and chemical weapons, and for adapting the treaty toolbox used to prevent the spread of those weapons.

title: Data Sharing and Global Public Health: Defining What We Mean by Data
authors: Nina Schwalbe, Brian Wahl, Jingyi Song, Susanna Lehtimaki
summary: As the volume of public health data expands and data become more interconnected, a broad range of data is being used to support research and inform global health policies and practice. This paper expands on an existing framework to classify data into four broad archetypes: patient data, health systems data, routine public health data, and health research data.

title: Artificial intelligence (AI) and the future of global health
authors: Nina Schwalbe, Brian Wahl
summary: Although AI-driven health interventions can help address several existing and emerging health challenges, many issues are not sufficiently described in the literature and warrant further exploration. These relate to the development of AI-driven health interventions, how efficacy is assessed and reported, planning for deployment at scale, and the ethical, regulatory, and economic standards that protect the interests of communities in low- and middle-income countries.

title: Accelerating access to medicines in a changing world
authors: Hannah Ketler, Susanna Lehtimaki, Nina Schwalbe
summary: Many access tools were designed and implemented by donors, with relatively little engagement from patients or interaction with the systems into which the product is or will be introduced.
source: Bulletin of the World Health Organization 2020

title: COVID-19: Rethinking risk
authors: Nina Schwalbe, Susanna Lehtimaki, Juan Pablo Gutiérrez
summary: Although older age and underlying conditions are visible markers of increased risk, people subject to structural inequities are more likely to develop underlying conditions and receive poor quality health care for management of those conditions and of COVID-19.

title: Why are we closing schools?
authors: Nina Schwalbe
summary: Keeping kids out of the classroom will make recovering from the pandemic harder in the long term, while not keeping us any safer in the near term. Reopening schools doesn't appear to meaningfully increase the level of risk faced by teachers or students, but closing them causes well-documented damage to students. Evidence from around the world shows that many schools should remain open, and officials should take more steps to open up classrooms.

title: Apples and oranges? Can second-generation vaccines become as low cost as generic medicines?
authors: Aurelia Nguyen, Nina Schwalbe
summary: A step change in cost will require fundamental shifts in vaccine technologies and how they are developed, regulated and even manufactured.

title: Expanding the use of community health workers in urban settings
authors: Brian Wahl, Susanna Lehtimaki, Stefan Germann, Nina Schwalbe
summary: As global and national policymakers deliberate approaches to achieving the SDGs, including universal health coverage, the delivery of community-based interventions involving community health workers in urban settings should be strongly considered.

title: Global Public Goods for Health (GPGs)
authors: Gavin Yamey, Jessica Kraus, Sara Fewer, Nina Schwalbe
summary: In a new policy paper, the authors examine the potential support for global public goods for health from four organizations that provide the most development assistance for health: Gavi, the Global Fund, World Bank, and World Health Organization.

title: Artificial intelligence (AI) and global health
authors: Brian Wahl, Aline Cossy-Gantner, Stefan Germann, Nina Schwalbe
summary: As resource-poor settings become more connected and the data they produce of higher quality, the ability of AI to address health challenges will likely expand.

title: Time's up for journal gender bias
authors: Nina Schwalbe, Jennifer Fearon
summary: From January 2013 through February 2018, The Lancet published the reports of 39 Commissions. Only 34% of all named commissioners have been women.

title: Maternal and child health and non-communicable diseases
authors: Luisa Brumana, Alvaro Arroyo, Nina Schwalbe, Susanna Lehtimaki, David Hipgrave
summary: Following a life-course approach, maternal and child health interventions, before delivery and during childhood and adolescence, can prevent non-communicable diseases.

title: Generation Men
authors: Nina Schwalbe
summary: The Fearless Girl statue that faces down Wall Street's charging bull grabbed international headlines and triggered a debate about the glass ceiling that continues to obstruct women.

title: Zero-Draft Framework for Tracking Implementation of the Pandemic Agreement
authors: Spark Street Advisors
summary: The Pandemic Agreement directs the Conference of Parties (COP) to create a mechanism to facilitate and strengthen implementation, including by monitoring key commitments and progress. This zero-draft framework is intended as a living tool with adaptive capacity to evolve with political and institutional developments, contributing to early discussions on reporting the COP will lead under Article 21.

title: Independent Monitoring for the Pandemic Agreement – A Proposal for Action
authors: Spark Street Advisors
summary: Based on evidence from monitoring other treaties, expert interviews, and analysis of various forms of independence, this report outlines the draft zero Terms of Reference for a Pandemic Agreement Independent Monitoring Committee. The primary purpose of an Independent Committee would be to verify the timeliness, completeness, and accuracy of Member State reports, complementing state self-reporting and peer review outlined in the current draft of the Pandemic Agreement.
source: Spark Street Advisors final report and policy brief

title: Independent Monitoring Mechanism for the Pandemic Accord - Accountability for a Safer World
authors: Spark Street Advisors
summary: This analysis features a proposal for independent monitoring of state compliance with an eventual pandemic accord, based on analysis of monitoring approaches to relevant international treaties, literature reviews, and in-depth interviews with 40 experts from around the world. It recommends an independent monitoring committee, fully autonomous and able to verify state reports through data triangulation, reporting to a body directly accountable to heads of state and government.

title: Independent Review and Investigation Mechanisms to Prevent Future Pandemics: A Proposed Way Forward
authors: Spark Street Advisors
summary: To inform the design of an accountability system for a pandemic treaty, this report explores institutional mechanisms with a mandate to review state compliance with key international agreements and conduct independent country investigations while managing sovereign considerations. It summarizes findings from a review of 19 international mechanisms and proposes combining periodic review, on-site investigations, non-negotiable design principles, and technical support.
source: Spark Street Advisors analysis and policy brief

title: HPV Vaccination in Out-of-school Context
authors: Spark Street Advisors
summary: HPV vaccination programs worldwide have primarily deployed school-based delivery strategies, with very little effort to reach girls who are temporarily or permanently out of school or beyond school age. This global synthesis reviews non-school delivery strategies in low- and middle-income countries for girls aged 9-19, and, with Ethiopia as a frontrunner country, develops an assessment tool to identify entry points, partners, and new approaches for reaching out-of-school girls with HPV vaccinations.
source: Spark Street Advisors global review, assessment tool, and Ethiopia report

title: Learning Organizations: Theory and Practice
authors: Spark Street Advisors
summary: This report explores organizational learning, summarizing theoretical and practical aspects. It examines key concepts, models, and enablers of learning that help organizations adapt and develop, and, by analyzing six global organizations including Gavi and the Global Fund, highlights how they apply a range of strategies and tools to foster a culture of learning.
